title: The Olive Tree and the Mystery of Israel's Future
summary: Paul insists that God has not rejected his people: as in Elijah's day, there is a remnant chosen by grace, while the rest have been hardened. Israel's stumbling has brought salvation to the Gentiles, and Paul warns Gentile believers, pictured as wild branches grafted into Israel's olive tree, not to boast over the natural branches. He reveals a mystery: Israel's partial hardening will last until the full number of the Gentiles comes in, and so all Israel will be saved. The chapter ends in a hymn of praise to the unsearchable wisdom of God.
story: Chapters 9 and 10 showed that God's word has not failed and that Israel is responsible for not believing. Chapter 11 answers the question these raise: has God then rejected his people? Paul's answer is a firm no, and he gives three reasons: there is a present remnant, Israel's stumbling is not final, and God's gifts and calling are irrevocable. This chapter completes the argument of chapters 9 to 11 and indeed of chapters 1 to 11, ending in worship. From chapter 12 onward Paul will draw out what this mercy means for daily life in the church.
historical:
Paul identifies himself in verse 1 as an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin. He is himself evidence that God has not rejected Israel. The church in Rome in the mid-50s AD included both Jewish and Gentile believers, but Gentiles were probably the majority, and Paul explicitly addresses them in verse 13. Some had evidently begun to think of themselves as the replacement for Israel, and Paul's warnings in verses 18 to 22 are aimed at that attitude.

The example of Elijah comes from 1 Kings 19, where the prophet, fleeing Jezebel after the contest on Mount Carmel, complains that he alone is left faithful, and God answers that he has kept seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal. Paul's quotations in verses 8 to 10 draw on Deuteronomy 29:4, Isaiah 29:10, and Psalm 69:22-23, and his closing quotations come from Isaiah 59:20-21, Isaiah 27:9, Isaiah 40:13, and Job 41:11.
cultural:
The olive tree was one of the chief crops of the Mediterranean, prized for oil used in food, lamps, medicine, and anointing. Israel's prophets used the olive as a picture of Israel itself (Jeremiah 11:16 calls Israel a green olive tree). Olive trees can live for centuries, and farmers maintained them by pruning and grafting. The usual practice was to graft a shoot of a cultivated olive onto wild stock. Paul's picture reverses this: a wild branch is grafted into a cultivated tree, and he himself says this is "contrary to nature" (verse 24). The unusual image makes his point: the Gentiles' place in God's people is pure grace, and they draw their life from Israel's root.

Verse 16 draws on the law of the firstfruits of dough in Numbers 15:17-21, where Israelites offered a portion of the first batch of dough to the Lord, and that offering consecrated the whole. The "root" is most often understood as the patriarchs (compare verse 28), though some take it as Christ or as God's covenant promise itself.
literary: Paul uses the same question formula twice ("I ask then", verses 1 and 11), each followed by an emphatic denial. The first section (verses 1-10) concerns the remnant and the hardening, the second (verses 11-24) the purpose of Israel's stumbling and the olive tree allegory addressed directly to Gentile readers, and the third (verses 25-32) the revealed mystery. The argument moves by "how much more" reasoning: if Israel's failure brought riches, how much more their fullness. The climax is a doxology (verses 33-36), a hymn of praise that combines exclamation, rhetorical questions from Isaiah and Job, and a final confession that all things are from, through, and to God.

outline.t: A remnant chosen by grace; the rest hardened
Israel's stumbling and the riches of the Gentiles
The olive tree: a warning against Gentile boasting
The mystery: all Israel will be saved
Praise for the depth of God's wisdom

doctrines.note: Verse 29 is the chapter's anchor: "God’s gifts and His call are irrevocable." God has not abandoned his covenant with Israel; the Gentiles are grafted into it rather than replacing it, and Israel remains beloved for the sake of the patriarchs.

Salvation for both Jews and Gentiles rests on mercy. Paul says God has shut all people up in disobedience so that he may have mercy on all, which does not mean every person will be saved, but that no one is saved except by mercy.

The olive tree shows the church as one people, rooted in Israel, into which Gentiles are grafted by faith. Gentile believers are warned against arrogance toward Jews, a warning the church has often failed to heed.

God works through Israel's stumbling, the Gentile mission, and Israel's future restoration to accomplish his purpose. The final hymn confesses that his judgments are unsearchable and his ways beyond tracing.

words.note: Leimma, remnant, what is left over. The idea runs through the prophets, who spoke of a faithful remnant surviving judgment. Paul says there is at the present time "a remnant chosen by grace" (verse 5), namely the Jewish believers in Jesus, himself included. The remnant is a sign that God has not abandoned the whole.

Porosis, hardening, a word used of the hardening of bone or of callused skin, and so of dulled understanding. In verse 25 Paul says "a hardening in part" has come to Israel. Both "in part" and "until" limit it: the hardening affects part of Israel and lasts for a period, not forever.

Egkentrizo, to graft in. It appears six times in verses 17 to 24, all in the olive tree picture. Grafting joins a branch to a living root so that it shares the root's life. The word stresses that Gentiles have no life of their own apart from the tree God planted, and that God can graft the natural branches in again.

Musterion, mystery. In Paul it doesn't mean a puzzle but a part of God's plan once hidden and now revealed. The mystery in verse 25 is the order of events: a partial hardening of Israel, the coming in of the Gentiles, and then the salvation of all Israel.

christ: Christ is present in this chapter mostly by implication, but decisively so. The remnant are those Jews who believe in him; the branches are broken off because of unbelief and grafted in by faith in him. Paul's quotation in verses 26 and 27 speaks of "The Deliverer" who "will come from Zion" and "remove godlessness from Jacob". Most interpreters understand the Deliverer as Christ, either at his first coming or, more commonly, at his return. The olive tree itself is rooted in the promises to the patriarchs that find their yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20). The chapter's closing hymn is addressed to God, but it mirrors what Paul elsewhere says of Christ, through whom all things exist (1 Corinthians 8:6; Colossians 1:16).

hard.q: What does Paul mean when he says "all Israel will be saved" (11:26)?
hard.a:
Interpreters read this verse in several ways. The most widely held view today takes "all Israel" as the Jewish people as a whole, not every individual but Israel as a people, turning to Christ in faith in the future, often connected with his return. This view points to the contrast in verse 25 between Israel and the Gentiles, which suggests Israel means ethnic Israel in the next verse as well, and to the language of the natural branches being grafted in again. A second view takes "all Israel" as the total number of elect Jews across history, the remnant gathered over time, so that the verse describes how God saves Israel through the whole age rather than at the end. A third view, held by John Calvin among others, takes "all Israel" as the whole people of God, Jews and Gentiles together, the Israel of God (Galatians 6:16).

A smaller group of modern interpreters has proposed that Israel will be saved by a separate covenant apart from faith in Christ. Most interpreters, across traditions, reject this because verse 23 conditions the grafting in again on not persisting in unbelief, and because the Deliverer comes to take away sins. Readers also differ on the meaning of "And so" at the start of verse 26: in this manner, or after this. Whatever view one takes, Paul's point is that God has not abandoned Israel, that Gentile believers have no ground for arrogance, and that God's mercy will have the last word. The chapter's own response is doxology, not a timetable.

questions: Paul warns Gentile believers, "do not boast over those branches". What are the ways Christians have boasted over the Jewish people, and what does this chapter say to them?
Paul insists that God's gifts and call are irrevocable. How does that shape your confidence in God's promises to you?
The argument of chapters 9 to 11 ends in worship rather than a neat answer. What might it look like to respond to hard questions in the same way?
